---
title: "Embeddings"
lang: en
---

In this chapter we introduce the central concepts of the thesis. We
introduce functions between partial orders such as embedding, complete
embedding, and dense embedding. We show that every dense embedding is
complete but not conversely. Under these embeddings between partial
orders — all of them in the ground model $V$ — we obtain generic
extensions of $V$ which, depending on the nature of the embedding, are
in some cases proper extensions, while in others the extensions produced
are the same. Finally, we prove that Cohen forcing embeds densely into
every countable, atomless partial order.

## Complete embeddings

For the rest of this chapter, $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ will always
denote two partial orders.

::: {#def-encaje}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be a function. We say that $e$ is an
**embedding** if for every $p, r \in \mathbb P$ the following hold:

1. $p \leq r$ implies $e(p) \leq e(r)$ — that is, $e$ preserves the
   order;
2. $p \perp r$ implies $e(p) \perp e(r)$ — that is, $e$ preserves
   incompatibility.
:::

Note that the term *embedding* should not be confused with an injective
function: if for example all elements of $\mathbb P$ are compatible (say
$\mathbb P$ is linearly ordered), then the function
$e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ given by
$e(p) = \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q}$ is a non-injective embedding.

**Notation.** If $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ is a function and
$X \subseteq \mathbb P$, we denote the direct image of $X$ by
$e\,{}''X$.

We are interested in embeddings that preserve maximal antichains.

::: {#def-encajecompleto}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be an embedding. We say that $e$ is
a **complete embedding** if for every maximal antichain $A$ in
$\mathbb P$, $e\,{}''A$ is a maximal antichain in $\mathbb Q$.
:::

**Notation.** Whenever there is a function $e$ between two partial
orders $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ as in @def-encajecompleto, we write
$\mathbb P \leq_c \mathbb Q$.

The next is an equivalence that will be useful later.

::: {#thm-equivalenciaencaje}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be an embedding. The following are
equivalent.

1. $e$ is a complete embedding.
2. For every $q \in \mathbb Q$ there is $p \in \mathbb P$ such that if
   $r \leq p$, then $e(r) \mid q$. In this case we say that $p$ is an
   **$e$-reduction** of $q$ to $\mathbb P$.
:::

::: {.proof}
It suffices to prove that preserving maximal antichains is equivalent
to every $q \in \mathbb Q$ having an $e$-reduction to $\mathbb P$.

We prove (1) implies (2) by contrapositive. So if (2) fails, there is
$q \in \mathbb Q$ such that for every $p \in \mathbb P$ there is
$r \leq p$ with $e(r) \perp q$. Let
$D = \{r \in \mathbb P : e(r) \perp q\}$. By our assumption, $D$ is
dense in $\mathbb P$. Consider $A \subseteq D$ a maximal antichain in
$D$. By @prp-amaximalendenso, $A$ is maximal in $\mathbb P$. Since $e$
preserves incompatibility, $e\,{}''A$ is an antichain. Now,
$q \notin e\,{}''A$, since otherwise $q \perp q$, which is impossible.
Moreover, $q \perp e(r)$ for every $r \in A$, that is,
$e\,{}''A \cup \{q\}$ is an antichain. But then $e\,{}''A \subsetneq
e\,{}''A \cup \{q\}$, so $e\,{}''A$ is not maximal.

We prove (2) implies (1) by contradiction. Let $A \subseteq \mathbb P$
be a maximal antichain in $\mathbb P$ for which $e\,{}''A$ is not a
maximal antichain in $\mathbb Q$. Then there is $q \in \mathbb Q$
incompatible with every element of $e\,{}''A$. Let $p$ be an
$e$-reduction of $q$ to $\mathbb P$. Since $A$ is a maximal antichain
in $\mathbb P$, $p \mid a$ for some $a \in A$. Let $r \leq p, a$. Then
$e(r) \leq e(a)$ and also $e(r) \mid q$. So $s \leq e(r), q$ for some
$s \in \mathbb Q$. But then $s \leq e(a), q$, that is, $e(a) \mid q$,
which is a contradiction since $e(a) \in e\,{}''A$.
:::

If $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ is a complete embedding and
$q \in \mathbb Q$, @thm-equivalenciaencaje guarantees that there is an
$e$-reduction $p$ of $q$ to $\mathbb P$. However, $p$ is not unique. For
instance, if $p_1 \leq p$, then for any $p_2 \leq p_1$ we have
$e(p_2) \mid q$, since $p_2 \leq p$. So $p_1$ is also an $e$-reduction
of $q$ to $\mathbb P$.

Returning to the embedding $e(p) = \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q}$, where all
elements of $\mathbb P$ are compatible, the equivalence of
@thm-equivalenciaencaje shows that our (non-injective) embedding is
complete. Indeed, if $q \in \mathbb Q$, then any $p \in \mathbb P$ is
an $e$-reduction of $q$ to $\mathbb P$, since
$e(r) = \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q} \geq q$ for every $r \leq p$. In
particular, $e(r) \mid q$.

The previous theorem characterises complete embeddings without
mentioning models of ZFC. In this context, and given our interests, the
following result is of central importance.

Before stating our theorem, note that if a function $f : \mathbb P \to
\mathbb Q$ is an element of $V$, then $\operatorname{dom} f \in V$,
since $\operatorname{dom} f$ is an absolute notion.

::: {#thm-encajeuno}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be an embedding with
$e, \mathbb P, \mathbb Q \in V$. The following are equivalent.

1. $e$ is complete.
2. For every $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic filter $H$, $e^{-1}[H]$ is a
   $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter and $V[e^{-1}[H]] \subseteq V[H]$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove (1) implies (2). Let $H$ be a $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic filter.
Let $G = e^{-1}[H]$ and show that $G$ satisfies the conditions of
@lem-filtroequivalencia. Let $p, q \in \mathbb P$.

If $p, q \in G$, then $e(p), e(q) \in H$. Since $H$ is a filter,
$e(p) \mid e(q)$. But since $e$ preserves incompatibility, $p \mid q$ —
that is, there is $r \in \mathbb P$ with $r \leq p, q$.

Suppose $p \in G$ and $p \leq q$. Then $e(p) \in H$,
$e(q) \in \mathbb Q$, and since $e$ is an embedding, $e(p) \leq e(q)$.
But then, since $H$ is a filter, $e(q) \in H$, so $q \in G$.

We prove the genericity of $G$ by contradiction. Suppose
$G \cap D = \emptyset$ for some $D \in V$ dense in $\mathbb P$. Observe
that this implies $H \cap e\,{}''D = \emptyset$. Indeed, if
$q \in H \cap e\,{}''D$, then $q \in H$ and $q = e(p)$ for some
$p \in D$, hence $e(p) \in H$ and therefore $p \in G$, that is,
$G \cap D \neq \emptyset$.

So $H \cap e\,{}''D = \emptyset$. Since $H$ is $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic,
by @lem-lemadenso (1) applied to $e\,{}''D$ there is $q \in H$ such
that $r \perp q$ for every $r \in e\,{}''D$ — that is,
$e(r') \perp q$ for every $r' \in D$. Since $e$ is complete, $q$ has a
reduction to $\mathbb P$, say $p'$. So $e(t) \mid q$ for any
$t \leq p'$, whence $t \notin D$, which is impossible since $D$ is
dense in $\mathbb P$.

We prove (2) implies (1) by contrapositive. Suppose there is
$q \in \mathbb Q$ that does not admit an $e$-reduction. By
@lem-condicionenG, there is a $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic filter $H$ with
$q \in H$. Define $D = \{p \in \mathbb P : e(p) \perp q\}$, which is a
dense subset of $\mathbb P$. Indeed, given any $r \in \mathbb P$, there
is $p \leq r$ with $e(p) \perp q$ ($p$ is not an $e$-reduction of $q$),
hence $p \in D$. Also, $D \in V$ because
$\mathbb P, e, q \in V$ (note $q \in V$ since $q \in \mathbb Q \in V$
and $V$ is transitive). However, $D \cap e^{-1}[H] = \emptyset$: if
$p \in D$, then $e(p) \perp q$, and since $q \in H$ we have
$e(p) \notin H$, i.e. $p \in D \setminus e^{-1}[H]$. So $e^{-1}[H]$ is
not a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter.

We now prove the containment of the generic extensions. Since
$e \in V \subseteq V[H]$ and $H \in V[H]$, we have $e^{-1}[H] \in V[H]$.
Therefore, by @lem-minimalidad, $V[e^{-1}[H]] \subseteq V[H]$.
:::

One way to read the previous theorem is: if
$\mathbb P \leq_c \mathbb Q$, then the generic extension given by
$\mathbb Q$ always contains the one given by $\mathbb P$.
Schematically:

$$
V \;\subseteq\; V[G] \;\subseteq\; V[H],
\qquad G = e^{-1}[H] \subseteq \mathbb P, \;\; H \subseteq \mathbb Q.
$$

::: {#cor-encaje-isomorfismo}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be an isomorphism with
$e, \mathbb P, \mathbb Q \in V$, and let $G \subseteq \mathbb P$. Then
$G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter if and only if $e\,{}''G$ is
a $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic filter.
:::

It is important to stress that if $\mathbb P$ is a suborder of
$\mathbb Q$ (see @def-suborden), it is not necessarily the case that
the generic extension given by $\mathbb Q$ contains the one given by
$\mathbb P$. An example is to take $\mathbb P := 2^{<\omega}$ and
$\mathbb Q := 2^{<\omega_1}$ (see the examples section in chapter 1).
In this case $\mathbb P$ is a suborder of $\mathbb Q$ and, by
@prp-unnuevoreal and @prp-nadanuevo, the forcing notion $\mathbb P$
adds a new function from $\omega$ to $2$ while $\mathbb Q$ does not,
so $\mathbb P$ cannot be completely embedded into $\mathbb Q$.

In the setting of @thm-encajeuno, it is natural to ask whether there is
a forcing notion in $V[e^{-1}[H]]$ that adds to this extension the
objects missing to recover $V[H]$. We answer this positively by first
introducing the concept of the quotient of a partial order modulo a
set.

::: {#def-moduloG}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be a complete embedding with
$e, \mathbb Q \in V$. For any $P \subseteq \mathbb P$, define
$$
\mathbb Q / P = \{q \in \mathbb Q :
                 \forall p \in P \, (e(p) \mid q)\}.
$$
:::

Recall that by @def-gamma,
$\Gamma = \{(\check{p}, p) : p \in \mathbb P\}$, while
@lem-gammaesg guarantees that $\Gamma_G = G$ for any
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter $G$ on $\mathbb P$. Since
$\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P} \in G$ for every such filter, it follows from
@thm-teoremadeforcing (2) that
$\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P} \Vdash \Gamma \subseteq \check{\mathbb P}$.
Now, since $\mathbb Q \in V$, $\mathbb Q$ has a canonical name
$\check{\mathbb Q}$ (see @def-nombrecanonico), so we can denote a
$\mathbb P$-name for the quotient $\mathbb Q/G$ by
$\check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma$.

::: {#prp-reduccion}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be a complete embedding with
$e, \mathbb P, \mathbb Q \in V$, and let $q \in \mathbb Q$. Then
$p \in \mathbb P$ is an $e$-reduction of $q$ to $\mathbb P$ if and
only if $p \Vdash \check{q} \in \check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Suppose $p$ is an $e$-reduction of $q$ to $\mathbb P$. Let $G$ be any
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter with $p \in G$, and let $r \in G$ be
arbitrary. Then there is $s \in G$ with $s \leq p, r$. Since
$s \leq p$, by hypothesis $e(s) \mid q$, that is, $t \leq e(s), q$ for
some $t \in \mathbb Q$. On the other hand, $e(s) \leq e(r)$ since $e$
is an embedding. So $e(s) \leq e(r), q$, hence $q \in \mathbb Q/G$.
Therefore $p \Vdash \check{q} \in \check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma$.

We prove the remaining implication by contrapositive. If $p$ is not a
reduction of $q$, then there is $r \leq p$ with $e(r) \perp q$. Let
$G$ be a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter with $r \in G$ (see
@lem-condicionenG). Since $G$ is a filter, $p \in G$. In summary,
$p \in G$ and $r \in G$ with $r \leq p$ and $e(r) \perp q$, that is,
$q \notin \mathbb Q/G$. Therefore
$p \nVdash \check{q} \in \check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma$.
:::

Normally the notation for the generic extension does not mention which
forcing notion produced it. However, in the next two theorems the
following situation arises: a set $S \subseteq \mathbb Q/G$ is
simultaneously a $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic filter and a
$(V[G], \mathbb Q/G)$-generic filter. For this reason we add a
subscript to the extension notation:
$V[S]_{\mathbb Q} = \{\dot x_S : \dot x \in V^{\mathbb Q}\}$, while
$V[G][S]_{\mathbb Q/G} = \{\dot x_S : \dot x \in
(V[G])^{\mathbb Q/G}\}$.

Note that if $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ is a complete embedding and
$G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter, then $\mathbb Q/G$ inherits
the order of $\mathbb Q$. Also, for each $p \in G$,
$e(p) \leq \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q}$ and therefore
$e(p) \mid \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q}$. Hence
$\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q} \in \mathbb Q/G$. Thus the triple
$(\mathbb Q/G, \leq, \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q})$ is a partial order, which
we always consider a suborder of $\mathbb Q$.

We are now in a position to show that there is a forcing notion in
$V[e^{-1}[H]]$ that equates the extensions in @thm-encajeuno.

::: {#thm-lorestante}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be a complete embedding with
$e, \mathbb P, \mathbb Q \in V$. If $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic
filter and $K$ is a $(V[G], \mathbb Q/G)$-generic filter, then:

1. $K$ is $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic.
2. $V[K]_{\mathbb Q} = V[G][K]_{\mathbb Q/G}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We verify the genericity of $K$. Let $D \in V$ be a dense subset of
$\mathbb Q$. We show that $D \cap (\mathbb Q/G)$ is dense in
$\mathbb Q/G$. Let $q_0 \in \mathbb Q/G$ be arbitrary. Since
$\mathbb Q/G \subseteq \mathbb Q$, $q_0 \in \mathbb Q \in V$. By the
transitivity of $V$, $q_0 \in V$. Then
$(\check{q}_0)_G \in (\check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma)_G$, and by
@thm-teoremadeforcing (2) there is $p_0 \in G$ with
$p_0 \Vdash \check{q}_0 \in \check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma$. Define
$$
E = \{p \in \mathbb P : \exists q \in \mathbb Q \,
      (q \leq q_0 \,\&\, q \in D \,\&\,
       p \Vdash \check{q} \in \check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma)\}.
$$

We claim $E$ is dense below $p_0$. Let $p_1 \leq p_0$. By
@prp-reduccion, $p_0$ is an $e$-reduction of $q_0$ to $\mathbb P$, so
$e(p_1) \mid q_0$. Let $q_1 \in \mathbb Q$ be a common extension of
$e(p_1)$ and $q_0$. By density of $D$, $q \leq q_1$ for some $q \in D$.
Take $p_2 \in \mathbb P$, an $e$-reduction of $q$. Then
$e(p_2) \mid q$ and, by @prp-reduccion,
$p_2 \Vdash \check{q} \in \check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma$. Let
$q_2 \leq e(p_2), q$. Since $q \leq q_1 \leq e(p_1)$,
$q_2 \leq e(p_2), e(p_1)$, hence $p_1 \mid p_2$. Let
$p \leq p_1, p_2$. Then $p \leq p_1$ and $p \in E$.

$E \in V$ because $\mathbb P, \mathbb Q, D, q_0 \in V$. Since
$p_0 \in G$, by @lem-lemadenso (2) $G \cap E \neq \emptyset$. Let
$p \in G \cap E$. Then $p \in G$ and there is $q \in \mathbb Q \cap D$
with $q \leq q_0$ and
$p \Vdash \check{q} \in \check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma$. By @def-forzar,
$\check{q}_G = q \in \mathbb Q/G$. So we have found an element
$q \in D \cap (\mathbb Q/G)$ with $q \leq q_0$, which proves the
density of $D \cap (\mathbb Q/G)$.

$D \cap (\mathbb Q/G) \in V[G]$ because $D \in V \subseteq V[G]$ and
$\mathbb Q/G \in V[G]$. Since $K$ is a $(V[G], \mathbb Q/G)$-generic
filter, $K \cap D \cap (\mathbb Q/G) \neq \emptyset$, hence
$K \cap D \neq \emptyset$, which proves the genericity of $K$.

We prove the equality in (2). Observe that if $p \in G$, then
$e(p) \in K$. Otherwise, by @lem-lemadenso (1) applied to $\{e(p)\}$
there would be $q \in K$ with $q \perp e(p)$, contradicting
$K \subseteq \mathbb Q/G$. This shows $G \subseteq e^{-1}[K]$. By
@thm-encajeuno, $e^{-1}[K]$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter, so
by @lem-filtrosiguales, $G = e^{-1}[K]$. So by @thm-encajeuno,
$V[G] \subseteq V[K]_{\mathbb Q}$. But then, by @lem-minimalidad,
$V[G][K]_{\mathbb Q/G} \subseteq V[K]_{\mathbb Q}$. On the other hand,
$V \subseteq V[G] \subseteq V[G][K]_{\mathbb Q/G}$ and
$K \in V[G][K]_{\mathbb Q/G}$. So by @lem-minimalidad,
$V[K]_{\mathbb Q} \subseteq V[G][K]_{\mathbb Q/G}$.
:::

Schematically: there is a forcing notion, $\mathbb Q/G$, such that
given a $(V, \mathbb Q/G)$-generic filter $K$, the same set is a
$(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic filter, and the extension obtained by forcing
with $\mathbb Q$ equals the one obtained by first forcing with
$\mathbb P$ and then with $\mathbb Q/G$:

$$
\begin{array}{lcl}
V \;\subseteq\; V[G] \;\subseteq\; V[G][K]_{\mathbb Q/G} &=& V[K]_{\mathbb Q}, \\
G = e^{-1}[K] \subseteq \mathbb P, & & K \subseteq \mathbb Q/G \subseteq \mathbb Q.
\end{array}
$$

We now show a result that may be thought of as the converse of the
previous theorem.

::: {#thm-primerreciproco}
If $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ is a complete embedding with
$e, \mathbb P, \mathbb Q \in V$, $H$ is a $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic
filter, and $G = e^{-1}[H]$, then:

1. $H \subseteq \mathbb Q/G$.
2. $H$ is a $(V[G], \mathbb Q/G)$-generic filter.
3. $V[H]_{\mathbb Q} = V[G][H]_{\mathbb Q/G}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove (1). Let $q \in H$ and $p \in G$ be arbitrary. Then
$q = e(p_0)$ for some $p_0 \in G$, hence $p \mid p_0$. Therefore
$e(p) \mid e(p_0)$ since $e$ is an embedding. We have shown that $q$
is compatible with the image under $e$ of every element of $G$, that
is, $q \in \mathbb Q/G$. By @thm-encajeuno, moreover, $G$ is a
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter.

(2). We verify the genericity of $H$. Let $D \in V[G]$ be a dense
subset of $\mathbb Q/G$. So $D \in V[G]$ implies the existence of
$\dot D \in V^{\mathbb P}$ with $\dot D_G = D$, and by
@thm-teoremadeforcing (2), for some $p_0 \in G$,
$p_0 \Vdash \dot D$ is dense in $\check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma$. Define
$$
E = \{q \in \mathbb Q : \exists p \in \mathbb P \,
                       \exists q_1 \in \mathbb Q \,
   [(p \Vdash \check q_1 \in \dot D) \,\&\, q \leq e(p) \,\&\, q \leq q_1]\}.
$$

We claim $E$ is dense below $e(p_0)$. Let $q_0 \leq e(p_0)$. Since
$e$ is a complete embedding, $q_0$ has an $e$-reduction to
$\mathbb P$, say $p_1$. So $e(p_1) \mid q_0$ and, by
@prp-reduccion, $p_1 \Vdash \check q_0 \in \check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma$.
Take $s \leq e(p_1), q_0$. Since $q_0 \leq e(p_0)$,
$s \leq e(p_1), e(p_0)$, hence $p_1 \mid p_0$. Let $p_2 \leq p_1, p_0$.
In this case, @lem-alguienmasfuerte guarantees that
$p_2 \Vdash (\check q_0 \in \check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma \,\&\,
\dot D$ is dense in $\check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma)$. That is,
$p_2 \Vdash \exists x \, (x \in \check{\mathbb Q} \,\&\, x \in \dot D
\,\&\, x \leq \check q_0)$. By @lem-nombreeneldominio (1), there are
$p \in \mathbb P$ and
$\dot s_1 \in \operatorname{dom} \check{\mathbb Q}$ such that
$p \leq p_2$ and $p \Vdash (\dot s_1 \in \dot D \,\&\,
\dot s_1 \leq \check q_0)$. Now, since
$\operatorname{dom} \check{\mathbb Q} = \{\check r : r \in \mathbb Q\}$,
$\dot s_1 \in \operatorname{dom} \check{\mathbb Q}$ implies
$\dot s_1 = \check q_1$ for some $q_1 \in \mathbb Q$. In summary,
$p \Vdash \check q_1 \in \dot D \subseteq \check{\mathbb Q}/\Gamma$
and $p \Vdash \check q_1 \leq \check q_0$. By @lem-condicionenG, we
can fix a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter $K$ with $p \in K$. Then
$p$ is an $e$-reduction of $q_1$ to $\mathbb P$ (see @prp-reduccion)
and $(\check q_1)_K = q_1 \leq (\check q_0)_K = q_0$, i.e.
$q_1 \leq q_0$. So $e(p) \mid q_1$, where $q_1 \leq q_0$. Then there
is $q \in \mathbb Q$ with $q \leq e(p), q_1$. So $q \leq q_0$ and
$q \in E$.

We have $E \in V$, since $\mathbb P, \mathbb Q, e \in V$ and
$\dot D$ is also an element of $V$ because, by definition,
$V^{\mathbb P}$ is the collection of all $\mathbb P$-names that are
elements of $V$. So by @lem-lemadenso (2),
$E \cap H \neq \emptyset$. Let $q \in E \cap H$. Then there are
$p \in \mathbb P$ and $q_1 \in \mathbb Q$ such that $q \leq e(p)$,
$q \leq q_1$, and $p \Vdash \check q_1 \in \dot D$. Now,
$q \leq e(p)$ and $q \leq q_1$ imply that $e(p)$ and $q_1$ are both
elements of $H$, since $q \in H$; and since $G = e^{-1}[H]$,
$p \in G$. This and $p \Vdash \check q_1 \in \dot D$ give
$(\check q_1)_G = q_1 \in D$. So $q_1 \in H \cap D$, which verifies
the genericity of $H$.

We prove (3). By hypothesis $G = e^{-1}[H]$ and $H$ is a
$(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic filter, so by @thm-encajeuno,
$V[G] \subseteq V[H]_{\mathbb Q}$. But then, by @lem-minimalidad,
$V[G][H]_{\mathbb Q/G} \subseteq V[H]_{\mathbb Q}$. Now, since
$H \in V[G][H]_{\mathbb Q/G}$ and
$V \subseteq V[G][H]_{\mathbb Q/G}$, by the same lemma
$V[H]_{\mathbb Q} \subseteq V[G][H]_{\mathbb Q/G}$, which proves the
equality of the extensions.
:::

## Dense embeddings

In this section we study embeddings whose image is a dense subset of
the codomain.

::: {#def-encajedenso}
We say that $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ is a **dense embedding** if
and only if $e$ is an embedding such that $e\,{}''\mathbb P$ is a
dense set in $\mathbb Q$.
:::

**Notation.** Whenever there is a function $e$ between two partial
orders $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ as in @def-encajedenso, we write
$\mathbb P \leq_d \mathbb Q$.

::: {#prp-densoimplicacompleto}
Every dense embedding is complete.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be a dense embedding. Using the
equivalence of @thm-equivalenciaencaje, it suffices to show that every
element of $\mathbb Q$ has an $e$-reduction to $\mathbb P$.

Let $q \in \mathbb Q$. Since $e\,{}''\mathbb P$ is dense in
$\mathbb Q$, there is $p \in \mathbb P$ with $e(p) \leq q$. Let
$r \leq p$. Then $e(r) \leq e(p)$ since $e$ is an embedding, so
$e(r) \leq q$, and in particular $e(r) \mid q$. So $p$ is the desired
$e$-reduction.
:::

At this point the reader might ask whether the converse holds. It does
not — not every complete embedding is dense, as we show next.

::: {#prp-fn-completo-no-denso}
Let $I_0, I_1$ be non-empty sets with $I_0 \subsetneq I_1$. Then the
function
$e : \operatorname{Fn}(I_0, 2) \to \operatorname{Fn}(I_1, 2)$ given by
$e(p) = p$ for each $p \in \operatorname{Fn}(I_0, 2)$ is a complete
embedding that is not dense.
:::

::: {.proof}
Our function $e : \operatorname{Fn}(I_0, 2) \to \operatorname{Fn}(I_1, 2)$
preserves order and incompatibility: on the one hand, if
$p, q \in \operatorname{Fn}(I_0, 2)$ satisfy $p \leq q$, then
$e(p) \leq e(q)$. On the other hand, if $p \perp q$, by
@lem-unionesfuncion $p \cup q$ is not a function. So $e(p) \cup e(q)$
is not a function, that is, $e(p) \perp e(q)$.

By the equivalence of @thm-equivalenciaencaje, it remains to show
that every element of $\operatorname{Fn}(I_1, 2)$ admits an
$e$-reduction to $\operatorname{Fn}(I_0, 2)$. Let
$q \in \operatorname{Fn}(I_1, 2)$. We claim $q \restriction I_0$ is
an $e$-reduction of $q$ to $\operatorname{Fn}(I_0, 2)$. Indeed, if
$r \leq q \restriction I_0$, we can decompose $q$ as
$q = q \restriction I_0 \cup q \restriction (I_1 \setminus I_0)$, so
$r \cup q = r \cup q \restriction (I_1 \setminus I_0)$, since
$q \restriction I_0 \subseteq r$. Since
$\operatorname{dom} r \cap \operatorname{dom}(q \restriction
(I_1 \setminus I_0)) = \emptyset$, $r \cup q$ is a function, so
$r \mid q$, which proves the claim.

We now show that our complete embedding
$e : \operatorname{Fn}(I_0, 2) \to \operatorname{Fn}(I_1, 2)$ is not
dense. Let $x \in I_1 \setminus I_0$. Define
$q_0 \in \operatorname{Fn}(I_1, 2)$ as $q_0 = \{(x, 0)\}$. Observe
that no extension of $q_0$ belongs to
$e\,{}''\operatorname{Fn}(I_0, 2)$. Otherwise, if $p_0 \leq q_0$ for
some $p_0 = e(p_0) \in e\,{}''\operatorname{Fn}(I_0, 2)$, then
$q_0 \subseteq p_0$, hence
$\operatorname{dom} q_0 \subseteq \operatorname{dom} p_0$, which
implies $x \in I_0$, impossible. So
$e\,{}''\operatorname{Fn}(I_0, 2)$ is not a dense subset of
$\operatorname{Fn}(I_1, 2)$.
:::

The next result asserts the existence of a dense embedding between
partial orders considered in the examples of chapter 1. In the last
section of this chapter we will prove a more general result whose
proof uses the Axiom of Choice. One of the virtues of the theorem
below is that no choice is needed to construct the embedding.

::: {#thm-ejemplodenso}
$\omega^{<\omega} \leq_d 2^{<\omega}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $t \in \omega^{<\omega}$. Then $t : n \to \omega$ for some
$n \in \omega$. Define $e(t)$ as follows:
$$
e(t) = \begin{cases}
\emptyset, & \text{if } n = 0, \\
\langle \underbrace{0\,0\,\cdots\,0}_{t(0) \text{ times}}\, 1\,
        \underbrace{0\,0\,\cdots\,0}_{t(1) \text{ times}}\, 1 \,\cdots\, 1\,
        \underbrace{0\,0\,\cdots\,0}_{t(n-1) \text{ times}}\, 1 \rangle,
& \text{if } n > 0.
\end{cases}
$$

In other words, when $t \neq \emptyset$, $e(t) \in 2^{<\omega}$ is
determined by:

- $\operatorname{dom} e(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} t(i) + n$; and
- for every $k \in \operatorname{dom} e(t)$, $e(t)(k) = 1$ iff there
  is $\ell < n$ such that $k = \sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) + \ell$.

We have thus defined a function
$e : \omega^{<\omega} \to 2^{<\omega}$.

Let $t, s \in \omega^{<\omega}$ with domains $n$ and $m$, respectively.
We verify that $e$ is a function that preserves order and
incompatibility and whose image is dense in $2^{<\omega}$.

Suppose $t \leq s$ and we prove $e$ preserves the order. So
$m \leq n$. This hypothesis implies that
$\operatorname{dom} e(s) \leq \operatorname{dom} e(t)$. If
$s = \emptyset$, then $e(s) = \emptyset$ and the inequality is
trivial. Suppose $s \neq \emptyset$, i.e. $0 < m \leq n$. Then:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{dom} e(t) &= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} t(i) + n \\
&= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{m-1} t(i) + \sum_{i=m}^{n} t(i) + n \\
&= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{m-1} s(i) + m + \sum_{i=m}^{n} t(i) + (n-m) \\
&= \operatorname{dom} e(s) + \textstyle\sum_{i=m}^{n} t(i) + (n-m).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\sum_{i=m}^{n} t(i) + (n-m) \geq 0$,
$\operatorname{dom} e(s) \leq \operatorname{dom} e(t)$.

Now, if $s = \emptyset$, then $e(s) = \emptyset$, hence
$e(t) \leq e(s)$. Suppose $s \neq \emptyset$ and we prove
$e(t) \leq e(s)$ by showing that for any
$k \in \operatorname{dom} e(s)$, $e(s)(k) = 1$ if and only if
$e(t)(k) = 1$.

Take $k \in \operatorname{dom} e(s)$ with $e(s)(k) = 1$. So
$k = \sum_{i=0}^{\ell} s(i) + \ell$ for some $\ell < m$. Since
$t \leq s$, $s(i) = t(i)$ for each $i \leq \ell$, so
$k = \sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) + \ell$ with $\ell < m \leq n$, which
implies $e(t)(k) = 1$.

Suppose now that $k \in \operatorname{dom} e(s)$ satisfies
$e(t)(k) = 1$. Then by the definition of $e$ there is $\ell < n$
with $k = \sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) + \ell$. We claim $\ell < m$.
Otherwise, if $\ell \geq m$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
k &= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{m-1} t(i) + \sum_{i=m}^{\ell} t(i) + \ell \\
&= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{m-1} s(i) + m + \sum_{i=m}^{\ell} t(i) + (\ell - m).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\operatorname{dom} e(s) = \sum_{i=0}^{m-1} s(i) + m$,
$k = \operatorname{dom} e(s) + \sum_{i=m}^{\ell} t(i) + (\ell - m)$,
with $\ell - m \geq 0$. But then $\operatorname{dom} e(s) \leq k$,
contradicting $k \in \operatorname{dom} e(s)$, so $\ell < m$. Then,
since $t \leq s$, $\sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) = \sum_{i=0}^{\ell} s(i)$,
so $k = \sum_{i=0}^{\ell} s(i) + \ell$ with $\ell < m$, that is,
$e(s)(k) = 1$.

We prove $e$ preserves incompatibility. Suppose $t \perp s$. Then
there is
$i \in \operatorname{dom} t \cap \operatorname{dom} s$ with
$t(i) \neq s(i)$. Let
$\ell = \min \{i \in \operatorname{dom} t \cap \operatorname{dom} s :
t(i) \neq s(i)\}$. Without loss of generality assume
$t(\ell) < s(\ell)$.

Then for $k = \sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) + \ell$ we have $e(t)(k) = 1$.
Observe $k \in \operatorname{dom} e(s)$. Otherwise, if
$k \geq \operatorname{dom} e(s)$:
$$
\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) + \ell \geq
\sum_{i=0}^{m-1} s(i) + m =
\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1} s(i) + \sum_{i=\ell}^{m-1} s(i) + m.
$$

Since $s(i) = t(i)$ for every $i < \ell$,
$$
\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) + \ell \geq
\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1} t(i) + \sum_{i=\ell}^{m-1} s(i) + m;
$$
hence $t(\ell) \geq \sum_{i=\ell}^{m-1} s(i) + (m - \ell)$, and in
particular $t(\ell) \geq s(\ell)$, contradicting
$t(\ell) < s(\ell)$.

We prove $e(s)(k) \neq 1$. Otherwise, if $e(s)(k) = 1$, then
$k = \sum_{i=0}^{r} s(i) + r$ for some $r < m$. We have the
following cases:

I. If $r = \ell$, then $\sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) = \sum_{i=0}^{\ell} s(i)$.
Since $t(i) = s(i)$ for every $i < \ell$, $t(\ell) = s(\ell)$, which
contradicts the definition of $\ell$.

II. If $r < \ell$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
k &= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) + \ell \\
&= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{r} t(i) + r +
   \sum_{i=r+1}^{\ell} t(i) + (\ell - r) \\
&= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{r} s(i) + r +
   \sum_{i=r+1}^{\ell} t(i) + (\ell - r) \\
&= k + \textstyle\sum_{i=r+1}^{\ell} t(i) + (\ell - r).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\sum_{i=r+1}^{\ell} t(i) \geq 0$ and $\ell - r > 0$,
$k < k$, a contradiction.

III. If $\ell < r$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
k &= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{r} s(i) + r \\
&= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{\ell} s(i) + \ell +
   \sum_{i=\ell+1}^{r} s(i) + (r - \ell) \\
&= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) + \ell +
   \sum_{i=\ell+1}^{r} s(i) + (r - \ell) \\
&= k + \textstyle\sum_{i=\ell+1}^{r} s(i) + (r - \ell).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\sum_{i=\ell+1}^{r} s(i) \geq 0$ and $r - \ell > 0$, $k < k$,
which is impossible.

So $e(t)(k) = 1$ and $e(s)(k) \neq 1$, that is,
$e(t) \perp e(s)$.

We prove $e\,{}''(\omega^{<\omega})$ is dense in $2^{<\omega}$. Let
$p \in 2^{<\omega}$. Then there is $n < \omega$ with
$n = \operatorname{dom} p$. Consider
$p^{-1}[1] = \{k < n : p(k) = 1\}$. If $p^{-1}[1] = \emptyset$, take
$t := \{(0, n+1)\}$. Then $e(t) = p^{\frown}1$ (see
@def-concatenacion (3)), hence $e(t) \leq p$. If
$p^{-1}[1] \neq \emptyset$, order this set as
$p^{-1}[1] = \{k_0, k_1, \ldots, k_m\}$, where:

- (i) $k_0 < k_1 < \cdots < k_m$,
- (ii) $m \leq n$.

Define $t : m + 2 \to \omega$ as follows:

- $t(0) = k_0$,
- $t(i+1) = k_{i+1} - k_i - 1$ for $i < m$,
- $t(m+1) = n - k_m - 1$.

Then:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{dom} e(t) &= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{m+1} t(i) + m + 2 \\
&= k_0 + (k_1 - k_0 - 1) + \cdots + (k_m - k_{m-1} - 1) +
   (n - k_m - 1) + m + 2 \\
&= n + 2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that by (ii) and the above,
$\operatorname{dom} p \leq \operatorname{dom} e(t)$.

We verify $e(t) \leq p$ by showing that for every $k < n$, $p(k) = 1$
if and only if $e(t)(k) = 1$.

**Observation.** For every $\ell \leq m$,
$\sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) = k_{\ell} - \ell$. Indeed,
$$
k_{\ell} = k_0 + (k_1 - k_0 - 1) + \cdots + (k_{\ell} - k_{\ell-1} - 1) + \ell.
$$
That is, $k_\ell = \sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) + \ell$.

Suppose $p(k) = 1$ for some $k < n$. Then $k \in p^{-1}[1]$, so
$k = k_j$ for some $j \leq m$. By the observation,
$k_j = \sum_{i=0}^{j} t(i) + j$, with $j < m + 2$. Therefore
$e(t)(k_j) = 1$.

Suppose now that $e(t)(k) = 1$ for some $k < n$. Then there is
$\ell < m + 2$ with $k = \sum_{i=0}^{\ell} t(i) + \ell$. By the
observation, if $\ell \leq m$, then $k \in p^{-1}[1]$. We prove
this inequality by contradiction: suppose $\ell = m + 1$. Then:
$$
\begin{aligned}
k &= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{m+1} t(i) + m + 1 \\
&= \textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{m} t(i) + t(m+1) + m + 1 \\
&= t(0) + \cdots + t(m) + t(m+1) + m + 1 \\
&= k_0 + (k_1 - k_0 - 1) + \cdots + (k_m - k_{m-1} - 1) +
   (n - k_m - 1) + m + 1 \\
&= n,
\end{aligned}
$$
contradicting $k < n$.
:::

Dense embeddings are important because if a forcing notion is densely
embedded in another, then the generic extensions given by these
notions coincide (in a sense to be made precise in
@thm-igualdadextensiones).

::: {#def-tildee}
Let $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ be two partial orders and
$e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ a function. For each
$X \subseteq \mathbb P$, define
$\tilde e(X) = \{q \in \mathbb Q : \exists p \in X \, (e(p) \leq q)\}$.
:::

Note that by the previous definition, for each
$X \subseteq \mathbb P$, $e\,{}''X \subseteq \tilde e(X)$. Indeed, if
$q \in e\,{}''X$, then $q = e(p)$ for some $p \in X$, hence
$q \in \tilde e(X)$.

::: {#thm-igualdadextensiones}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be a dense embedding. If
$e, \mathbb P, \mathbb Q \in V$, then:

1. If $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter, then $\tilde e(G)$ is
   a $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic filter and $G = e^{-1}[\tilde e(G)]$.
   In this case, $V[G] = V[\tilde e(G)]$.
2. If $H \subseteq \mathbb Q$ is a $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic filter,
   then $e^{-1}[H]$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter and
   $H = \tilde e(e^{-1}[H])$. In this case, $V[e^{-1}[H]] = V[H]$.
:::

::: {.proof}
(1). We prove $\tilde e(G)$ is a filter. Let
$q_1, q_2 \in \tilde e(G)$. Then $e(p_1) \leq q_1$ and
$e(p_2) \leq q_2$ for some $p_1, p_2 \in G$. Since $G$ is a filter,
there is $p \in G$ with $p \leq p_1, p_2$. Hence
$e(p) \leq e(p_1), e(p_2)$. So $e(p) \in \tilde e(G)$ and
$e(p) \leq q_1, q_2$.

Let $r \in \tilde e(G)$ and $q \in \mathbb Q$ with $r \leq q$. Then
$e(p) \leq r$ for some $p \in G$. Hence $e(p) \leq q$, so
$q \in \tilde e(G)$.

We verify the genericity of $\tilde e(G)$. Let $D \in V$ be a dense
subset of $\mathbb Q$, and let
$$
E = \{p \in \mathbb P : \exists q \in D \, (e(p) \leq q)\}.
$$

We prove $E$ is dense in $\mathbb P$. Let $p \in \mathbb P$. Since
$D$ is dense in $\mathbb Q$ and $e(p) \in \mathbb Q$, $q \leq e(p)$
for some $q \in D$. By hypothesis, $e\,{}''\mathbb P$ is dense in
$\mathbb Q$, so $e(r) \leq q$ for some $r \in \mathbb P$. Then
$e(r) \leq e(p)$, in particular $e(r) \mid e(p)$, hence $r \mid p$.
Let $s \leq r, p$. Then $e(s) \leq q$ with $q \in D$, and $s \leq p$.
So $E$ is dense in $\mathbb P$.

Since $\mathbb P, D, e \in V$, $E \in V$. So
$G \cap E \neq \emptyset$, hence there are $p \in G$ and $q \in D$
with $e(p) \leq q$. So $q \in \tilde e(G)$. Therefore
$\tilde e(G) \cap D \neq \emptyset$.

We verify that $G = e^{-1}[\tilde e(G)]$. As shown, $\tilde e(G)$ is
a $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic filter, so by @thm-encajeuno and
@prp-densoimplicacompleto, $e^{-1}[\tilde e(G)]$ is a
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter. Now,
$e(G) \subseteq \tilde e(G)$, equivalently
$G \subseteq e^{-1}[\tilde e(G)]$. So by @lem-filtrosiguales,
$e^{-1}[\tilde e(G)] = G$.

Let $H = \tilde e(G)$ and we show $V[G] = V[H]$. By the previous
paragraph, $H$ is a $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic filter, hence by
@thm-encajeuno, $V[G] \subseteq V[H]$. Now, $H \in V[G]$ since
$G \in V[G]$ and $e, \mathbb P, \mathbb Q \in V \subseteq V[G]$. So
by @lem-minimalidad, $V[H] \subseteq V[G]$, and the equality holds.

(2). Since by @prp-densoimplicacompleto $e$ is a complete embedding,
by @thm-encajeuno, $e^{-1}[H]$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter.

Now, by (1), $\tilde e(e^{-1}[H])$ is a $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic
filter. Observe $\tilde e(e^{-1}[H]) \subseteq H$: if
$q \in \tilde e(e^{-1}[H])$, then $e(p) \leq q$ for some
$p \in e^{-1}[H]$, hence $e(p) \in H$, so $q \in H$ since $H$ is a
filter. So $\tilde e(e^{-1}[H])$ is a $(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic
filter contained in $H$, which by hypothesis is a
$(V, \mathbb Q)$-generic filter. So by @lem-filtrosiguales,
$H = \tilde e(e^{-1}[H])$.

Let $G = e^{-1}[H]$ and we show $V[G] = V[H]$. By @thm-encajeuno,
$V[G] \subseteq V[H]$. By hypothesis and the previous paragraph,
$H = \tilde e(G)$. Since $G \in V[G]$ and
$e, \mathbb P, \mathbb Q \in V \subseteq V[G]$, $H \in V[G]$. So by
@lem-minimalidad, $V[H] \subseteq V[G]$, hence $V[G] = V[H]$.
:::

Schematically, @thm-igualdadextensiones states that the two operations
$\tilde e(\cdot)$ and $e^{-1}[\cdot]$ are inverse to each other in the
appropriate sense, and that the generic extensions produced by
$\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ coincide:
$$
V[G] = V[\tilde e(G)], \qquad V[e^{-1}[H]] = V[H].
$$

By @thm-ejemplodenso, $\omega^{<\omega} \leq_d 2^{<\omega}$. So an
immediate corollary of @thm-igualdadextensiones is that
$\omega^{<\omega}$ and $2^{<\omega}$ produce the same forcing
extensions. However, the converse does not necessarily hold: two
forcing notions can produce the same generic extensions without being
densely embedded one in the other. To verify this we consider the
mentioned partial orders and show that there is no dense embedding of
$2^{<\omega}$ into $\omega^{<\omega}$.

Before that, we prove that complete embeddings preserve non-trivial
maximal antichains.

::: {#lem-atrivialenatrivial}
If $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ is a complete embedding and
$A \subseteq \mathbb P$ is a non-trivial maximal antichain in
$\mathbb P$, then $e\,{}''A$ is a non-trivial maximal antichain in
$\mathbb Q$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $A$ be a non-trivial maximal antichain in $\mathbb P$. Since $e$
is a complete embedding, $e\,{}''A$ is a maximal antichain (see
@def-encajecompleto). By hypothesis $A$ is not the trivial antichain,
so there are at least two incompatible elements $p, q \in A$. But
then $e(p) \perp e(q)$, hence $e(p) \neq e(q)$. So $e\,{}''A$ is not
trivial.
:::

::: {#prp-2omega-no-c-en-omega}
$2^{<\omega} \nleq_c \omega^{<\omega}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We first prove that $2^{<\omega}$ admits finite non-trivial maximal
antichains.

Let $p := \{(0, 0)\}$ and $q := \{(0, 1)\}$, and let $A = \{p, q\}$.
We show $A$ is a maximal antichain. By definition $p \neq q$.
Moreover $p \cup q$ is not a function, so by @lem-unionesfuncion
applied to our case, $p \perp q$. So $A$ is an antichain.

We prove $A$ is maximal by showing it satisfies the equivalence of
@prp-equivalencia. Let $r \in 2^{<\omega}$ be arbitrary. Then there
is $n < \omega$ with $\operatorname{dom} r = n$. If $n = 0$, $r$ is
the empty function, so $r$ is compatible with any element of $A$.
Suppose $n > 0$. Then $0 \in \operatorname{dom} r$, so
$r(0) \in \{0, 1\}$. If $r(0) = 0$, then $p \subseteq r$, i.e.
$r \leq p$, and since $r \leq r$, $r \leq p, r$. So $r \mid p$. If
$r(0) = 1$, then $q \subseteq r$, i.e. $r \leq q$, hence
$r \leq q, r$. So $r \mid q$.

We prove the proposition by contradiction. If
$2^{<\omega} \leq_c \omega^{<\omega}$, then there is a complete
embedding $e : 2^{<\omega} \to \omega^{<\omega}$. But then, if $B$ is
a finite non-trivial maximal antichain in $2^{<\omega}$, by
@lem-atrivialenatrivial, $e\,{}''B$ is a finite non-trivial maximal
antichain in $\omega^{<\omega}$. So it remains to show that no
finite non-trivial antichain in $\omega^{<\omega}$ can be maximal.

Let $B$ be a finite non-trivial antichain in $\omega^{<\omega}$.
Since $B \subseteq \omega^{<\omega} \setminus \{\emptyset\}$,
$0 \in \operatorname{dom} b$ for every $b \in B$. Consider
$\{r(0) : r \in B\} \subseteq \omega$, which is finite since $B$ is
finite. Take $k \in \omega \setminus \{r(0) : r \in B\}$. So if
$s = \{(0, k)\}$ and $t \in B$, then by definition
$s(0) = k \neq t(0)$. But then $s \perp t$, and since $t$ was
arbitrary, $s \notin B$. So $B \cup \{s\}$ is an antichain in
$\omega^{<\omega}$ properly containing $B$. So $B$ is not maximal.
:::

By @thm-ejemplodenso, @thm-igualdadextensiones, and the previous
result, we have exhibited two forcing notions that produce the same
extensions but where neither is densely embedded in the other.
Indeed, if $2^{<\omega} \leq_d \omega^{<\omega}$, since every dense
embedding is complete (see @prp-densoimplicacompleto),
$2^{<\omega} \leq_c \omega^{<\omega}$, which is impossible by the
previous proposition.

There is a type of partial order that is interesting because it
preserves a notion of interest, namely the $\kappa$-cc orders, whose
virtue is to preserve cofinalities greater than or equal to an
infinite cardinal $\kappa$ (the reader is invited to consult
[@kunen, Lemma 6.9, p. 213]).

::: {#def-kappacc}
Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal. We say that $\mathbb P$ has the
**$\kappa$-cc** if every antichain in $\mathbb P$ has cardinality
less than $\kappa$.
:::

The next result shows that whenever there is a dense embedding
between two notions $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$, the size of the
antichains in both orders does not exceed $\kappa$.

::: {#prp-kappa-cc-preservada}
$\mathbb P \leq_d \mathbb Q$ implies that $\mathbb P$ is $\kappa$-cc
if and only if $\mathbb Q$ is $\kappa$-cc.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be a dense embedding. Suppose
$\mathbb P$ has the $\kappa$-cc and we prove $\mathbb Q$ is
$\kappa$-cc. Let $A \subseteq \mathbb Q$ be an antichain. Since
$e\,{}''\mathbb P$ is a dense subset of $\mathbb Q$, for each
$a \in A$ there is $p_a \in \mathbb P$ with $e(p_a) \leq a$. Let
$B = \{p_a : a \in A\}$. We observe that $B$ is an antichain in
$\mathbb P$. Indeed, if $a \neq b$, then $p_a \perp p_b$: otherwise,
$p_a \mid p_b$, hence $e(p_a) \mid e(p_b)$, so
$q \leq e(p_a), e(p_b)$ for some $q \in \mathbb Q$. But then
$q \leq a, b$ since $e(p_a) \leq a$ and $e(p_b) \leq b$,
contradicting that $A$ is an antichain. So $B$ is an antichain and
therefore $|B| < \kappa$.

Now, let $f : A \to B$ be the function $f(a) = p_a$ for each
$a \in A$. We observe that $f$ is a bijection between $A$ and $B$.
Indeed, $f$ is injective because if $a \neq b$, we have seen above
that $p_a \perp p_b$, in particular $p_a \neq p_b$. Also $f$ is
surjective because every element of $B$ is, by definition of $f$,
the image of some element of $A$. So $|A| = |B|$ and, since
$|B| < \kappa$, the result follows.

We prove the remaining implication. Let $A \subseteq \mathbb P$ be
an antichain. Observe that $e \restriction A$ is an injective
function: if $e(p) = e(q)$ with $p, q \in A$, then in particular
$e(p) \mid e(q)$, hence $p \mid q$, which implies $p = q$ since $A$
is an antichain. Now, by @def-encajecompleto, $e\,{}''A$ is an
antichain in $\mathbb Q$, hence $|e\,{}''A| < \kappa$ since
$\mathbb Q$ is $\kappa$-cc. So $e \restriction A$ is an injection
from $A$ to $e\,{}''A$ with $|e\,{}''A| < \kappa$, hence
$|A| < \kappa$.
:::

::: {#def-kappacerrado}
We say that $\mathbb P$ is **$\kappa$-closed** if every decreasing
sequence $\langle p_\xi : \xi < \lambda \rangle$ of conditions in
$\mathbb P$ has a lower bound in $\mathbb P$, for any
$\lambda \leq \kappa$.
:::

$\kappa$-closed orders are interesting because they do not add new
subsets of $\kappa$ — in other words, if $\mathbb P \in V$ and $G$ is
a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter, then
$V[G] \cap {}^{\kappa}\omega \subseteq V$. A proof of this is
analogous to the proof of @prp-nadanuevo.

The following is an example of two forcing notions, one densely
embedded in the other, where one is $\kappa$-closed but the other is
not.

::: {#exm-kappacerrado-no-preservado}
There exist $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ such that $\mathbb P$ is
$\kappa$-closed, $\mathbb P \leq_d \mathbb Q$, and yet $\mathbb Q$ is
not $\kappa$-closed.
:::

We illustrate this by taking $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$, two subsets
of $\omega^{<\omega}$ (both seen as suborders of $\omega^{<\omega}$),
as follows:

(1) $\mathbb P$ consists of all functions whose domain is $\leq 1$,
i.e. $p \in \mathbb P$ if and only if $p = \emptyset$ or there exists
$n \in \omega$ with $p = \{(0, n)\}$. The order on $\mathbb P$ is the
one inherited from $\omega^{<\omega}$, so $\mathbb P$ has the shape
of a star tree with root $\emptyset$ and leaves $\{(0, n)\}$ for
each $n \in \omega$.

(2) Let $f \in {}^{\omega}\omega$ be the constant zero function:
$f(k) = 0$ for every $k \in \omega$. Set
$$
\mathbb Q = \{\emptyset\} \cup
            \{(f \restriction n)^{\frown} k :
              n \in \omega \,\&\, k \in \{0, 1\}\}.
$$
As with $\mathbb P$, the order on $\mathbb Q$ is inherited from
$\omega^{<\omega}$. Visually, $\mathbb Q$ is an "oblique" binary
tree: at each level $n$ the children are $f \restriction (n+1)$
(which continues the central branch of zeros) and
$(f \restriction n)^{\frown}1$ (a leaf).

We claim the following properties hold:

- (i) If $p, q \in \mathbb P$ and $p < q$, then $q = \emptyset$.
- (ii) $\mathbb P$ is $\omega$-closed.
- (iii) $\mathbb P \leq_d \mathbb Q$.

Property (i) holds: if, contrary to the claim, $q \neq \emptyset$,
then $0 \in \operatorname{dom} q$, so there is $m \in \omega$ with
$q = \{(0, m)\}$. Since $p < q$ and by the definition of
$\mathbb P$, $p = q$, impossible.

We prove (ii) by showing that if
$\langle p_i : i \in \omega \rangle$ is a decreasing sequence of
conditions in $\mathbb P$, then there are $m \in \omega$ and
$p \in \mathbb P$ with $p_n = p$ for every $n \geq m$. Otherwise,
for every $m \in \omega$ there is $n \geq m$ with $p_n \neq p_m$.
In particular, for $m = 0$ there is $p_n \neq p_0$ for some
$n \geq 0$. Note $n > 0$. So $p_n < p_0$, since $p_n \neq p_0$ and
both are elements of a decreasing sequence (note that since $p_n$ is
a proper extension of $p_0$, $0 \in \operatorname{dom} p_n$). But
then, for every $k \geq n$, $p_k \leq p_n$ (so
$0 \in \operatorname{dom} p_k$), in particular
$p_k(0) = p_n(0)$, hence $p_n = p_k$, impossible. So every
decreasing sequence in $\mathbb P$ has a lower bound — that is,
$\mathbb P$ is $\omega$-closed.

We prove (iii). Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be defined by
$e(p) = \emptyset$ if $p = \emptyset$ and
$e(\{(0, n)\}) = (f \restriction n)^{\frown} 1$ for each
$n \in \omega$.

We verify $e$ is a dense embedding. First, $e$ preserves the order.
Let $p, q \in \mathbb P$ with $p \leq q$. If $p < q$, by claim (i),
$q = \emptyset$. Hence $e(q) = \emptyset$, so $e(p) \leq e(q)$. If
$p = q$, then $e(p) = e(q)$ and the order is preserved.

We prove $e$ preserves incompatibility. Let $p, q \in \mathbb P$
with $p \perp q$. Observe that neither is $\emptyset$, since every
condition in $\mathbb P$ is compatible with $\emptyset$. So there
are $n, m \in \omega$ with $p = \{(0, n)\}$ and $q = \{(0, m)\}$.
Without loss of generality assume $n < m$. Then $e(p)(n) = 1$ and
$e(q)(n) = 0$ since $n < m$. So $e(p) \perp e(q)$.

Finally, we prove $e\,{}''\mathbb P$ is dense in $\mathbb Q$. Let
$q \in \mathbb Q$. If $q = \emptyset$, the image under $e$ of any
element of $\mathbb P$ is an extension of $q$. If
$q \neq \emptyset$, there is $n \in \omega$ with
$q = (f \restriction n)^{\frown} k$ with $k \in \{0, 1\}$. If
$q = (f \restriction n)^{\frown} 0$, then
$q = f \restriction (n+1)$, hence
$(f \restriction (n+1))^{\frown} 1 = e(\{(0, n+1)\})$ and
$e(\{(0, n+1)\}) \leq q$. If $q = (f \restriction n)^{\frown} 1$,
then $q = e(\{(0, n)\})$ and the result holds.

By @thm-igualdadextensiones, $\mathbb P \leq_d \mathbb Q$ implies
that the generic extensions given by $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$
coincide. So, by the previous example, if $\mathbb P$ is
$\kappa$-closed and $\mathbb P \leq_d \mathbb Q$, then $\mathbb Q$
does not add new subsets of $\kappa$ even though $\mathbb Q$ is not
necessarily $\kappa$-closed.

We now turn to partial orders called $\kappa$-distributive. These
orders are interesting because they do not add new functions from
$\kappa$ to $2$ (a proof can be found in
[@jech, Theorem 15.6, p. 228]). We know from @prp-nadanuevo that
$2^{<\omega_1}$ does not add a new real when $\kappa = \omega$, so
the natural question is whether this partial order is
$\omega$-distributive.

::: {#def-abierto-kappadistributivo}
Let $\mathbb P$ be a partial order.

1. A subset $U \subseteq \mathbb P$ is called **open** if for every
   $p \in U$ and $q \leq p$, $q \in U$.
2. If $\kappa$ is an infinite cardinal, $\mathbb P$ is
   **$\kappa$-distributive** if for every sequence
   $\{D_\alpha : \alpha < \kappa\}$ of open dense subsets of
   $\mathbb P$, $\bigcap_{\alpha < \kappa} D_\alpha$ is dense.
:::

Note that the intersection of $\kappa$ open dense subsets is always
open. Indeed, if $\{D_\alpha : \alpha < \kappa\}$ is such a
collection and $D = \bigcap_{\alpha < \kappa} D_\alpha$, then $D$
is open: if $p \in D$ and $q \leq p$, then $p \in D_\alpha$ for
every $\alpha < \kappa$, hence (since each $D_\alpha$ is open)
$q \in D_\alpha$, so $q \in D$.

::: {#lem-cerrado-implica-distributivo}
If $\mathbb P$ is $\kappa$-closed, then $\mathbb P$ is
$\kappa$-distributive.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $\{D_\alpha : \alpha < \kappa\}$ be a sequence of open dense
subsets of $\mathbb P$. We verify that
$D = \bigcap_{\alpha < \kappa} D_\alpha$ is dense in $\mathbb P$. By
induction on $\alpha < \kappa$ we prove that there exists
$\langle p_\alpha : \alpha < \kappa \rangle$ such that:

- (i) $p_0 \leq p$,
- (ii) for every $\alpha < \kappa$, $p_\alpha \in D_\alpha$; and
- (iii) if $\alpha < \beta < \kappa$, then $p_\beta \leq p_\alpha$.

Let $p \in \mathbb P$. Then there is $p_0 \in D_0$ with
$p_0 \leq p$. Suppose now that for some $\alpha < \kappa$ the
sequence $\langle p_\xi : \xi < \alpha \rangle$ satisfies (i), (ii)
and (iii). Since $\mathbb P$ is $\kappa$-closed, there is
$r \in \mathbb P$ with $r \leq p_\xi$ for every $\xi < \alpha$. By
density of $D_\alpha$, there is $p_\alpha \in D_\alpha$ with
$p_\alpha \leq r$. So $p_\alpha \leq p_\xi$ and
$p_\alpha \in D_\alpha$. This completes the induction. So, since
$\mathbb P$ is $\kappa$-closed, there is $q \in D$ with
$q \leq p_\alpha$ for every $\alpha < \kappa$. So $q \leq p$ and
$q \in D$.
:::

By the proof of @prp-nadanuevo, $2^{<\omega_1}$ is $\omega$-closed.
So by the previous lemma, $2^{<\omega_1}$ is $\omega$-distributive.

The next result shows that $\kappa$-distributivity is preserved under
dense embeddings.

::: {#prp-distributividad-preservada}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ be a dense embedding. Then:

1. If $D$ is an open dense subset of $\mathbb Q$, then $e^{-1}[D]$
   is an open dense subset of $\mathbb P$.
2. If $\mathbb P$ is $\kappa$-distributive, then $\mathbb Q$ is
   $\kappa$-distributive.
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove (1). Let $p \in e^{-1}[D]$ and $q \in \mathbb P$ with
$q \leq p$. Then $e(p) \in D$ and $e(q) \leq e(p)$. Since $D$ is
open in $\mathbb Q$, $e(q) \in D$, hence $q \in e^{-1}[D]$. So
$e^{-1}[D]$ is open. We verify $e^{-1}[D]$ is dense in $\mathbb P$.
Let $p \in \mathbb P$. Then $e(p) \in \mathbb Q$, and by density of
$D$, $q \leq e(p)$ for some $q \in D$. Since $e\,{}''\mathbb P$ is
dense in $\mathbb Q$, $e(p_0) \leq q$ for some $p_0 \in \mathbb P$.
Hence $e(p_0) \leq e(p)$, in particular $e(p_0) \mid e(p)$, so
$p_0 \mid p$. Let $p_1 \leq p_0, p$. Then $e(p_1) \leq e(p_0)$, and
since $e(p_0) \leq q$, $e(p_1) \leq q$, hence $e(p_1) \in D$ since
$q \in D$. So $p_1 \in e^{-1}[D]$ and $p_1 \leq p$.

We prove (2). Let $\{D_\alpha : \alpha < \kappa\}$ be a sequence of
open dense subsets of $\mathbb Q$. Let
$D = \bigcap_{\alpha < \kappa} D_\alpha$ and verify the density of
$D$. Let $q \in \mathbb Q$. Then $e(p_0) \leq q$ for some
$p_0 \in \mathbb P$. Since each $D_\alpha$ is open and dense, by (1)
$\{e^{-1}[D_\alpha] : \alpha < \kappa\}$ is a collection of open
dense subsets of $\mathbb P$. Since $\mathbb P$ is
$\kappa$-distributive, $E = \bigcap_{\alpha < \kappa} e^{-1}[D_\alpha]$
is an open dense subset of $\mathbb P$. So there is $p \in E$ with
$p \leq p_0$. Then $e(p) \in D$, $e(p) \leq e(p_0)$, and since
$e(p_0) \leq q$, the result follows.
:::

## Adding a Cohen real

Our main goal in this section is to prove that $\omega^{<\omega}$
embeds densely in every countable atomless forcing notion (in the
sense of @def-ordennoatomico). So forcing with any such notion is
equivalent to forcing with $\operatorname{Fn}(\omega, 2)$, i.e. the
forcing notion that adds a Cohen real. The proof of this result will
be divided into a series of lemmas.

::: {#def-downarrow}
Let $p \in \mathbb P$. Define
$p^{\downarrow} = \{r \in \mathbb P : r \leq p\}$.
:::

::: {#lem-anticadenas}
Let $\mathbb P$ be an atomless partial order. Let $p, q \in \mathbb P$
be compatible. Then there is $A \subseteq \mathbb P$ such that:

1. $A$ is an infinite antichain;
2. for every $r \in \mathbb P$, if $r \leq p$ then there is $a \in A$
   compatible with $r$;
3. there is an element $a_0 \in A$ with $a_0 \leq q$; and
4. $A \subseteq p^{\downarrow}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
There is $t \in \mathbb P$ with $t \leq p, q$.

We claim there exist
$\langle r_i : i \in \omega \rangle \subseteq \mathbb P$ and
$\langle s_i : i \in \omega \rangle \subseteq \mathbb P$ such that:

- (a) $\langle r_i : i \in \omega \rangle$ is decreasing,
- (b) $s_{i+1} \leq r_i$ for every $i \in \omega$, and
- (c) $r_i \perp s_i$ for every $i \in \omega$.

Since $\mathbb P$ is atomless and $t \in \mathbb P$, there are
$r_0, s_0 \in \mathbb P$ with $r_0, s_0 \leq t$ and $r_0 \perp s_0$.
Suppose for some $n \in \omega$ there exist
$\langle r_i : i \leq n \rangle$ and
$\langle s_i : i \leq n \rangle$ satisfying (a), (b) and (c). Again,
since $\mathbb P$ is atomless, there are
$r_{n+1}, s_{n+1} \in \mathbb P$ with $r_{n+1}, s_{n+1} \leq r_n$ and
$r_{n+1} \perp s_{n+1}$, completing the induction.

Let $B = \{s_i : i \in \omega\}$. We show $B$ is an antichain.
Suppose, seeking a contradiction, that there are $n, m$ with $m < n$
and $s_n \mid s_m$. Then there is $s \leq s_n, s_m$. By construction
$s_n \leq r_m$, so $s \leq r_m, s_m$, contradicting clause (c) of
the previous claim. So any two elements of $B$ with distinct indices
are incompatible — that is, $B$ is an antichain. $B$ is infinite
because, given two distinct indices $n$ and $m$, $s_n \perp s_m$
hence $s_n \neq s_m$.

By @prp-extenderanticadenamaximal, $B$ can be extended to an
infinite maximal antichain in $p^{\downarrow}$, say $A$. We verify
that $A$ also satisfies conditions (2) and (3).

To verify (2), let $r \in p^{\downarrow}$ be arbitrary. Since $A$
is a maximal antichain in $p^{\downarrow}$, by @prp-equivalencia
there is $a \in A$ with $a \mid r$.

Finally, $A$ satisfies (3) because $B \subseteq A$ and
$s \leq t \leq q$ for every $s \in B$.
:::

The construction of the antichain $B$ in @lem-anticadenas can be
visualised as a tree rooted at $t$ with, at each step, a fork
$r_i \perp s_i$. The "left" branch keeps refining
($r_{i+1} \leq r_i$), while each $s_i$ remains as a candidate
element for the antichain $B$.

Note that the previous result implies that every atomless partial
order is infinite.

For the next four results we consider a countable atomless partial
order $\mathbb P$ and identify it as
$\mathbb P = \{p_n : n \in \omega\}$, where for every
$n, m \in \omega$, $n \neq m$ implies $p_n \neq p_m$ and where
$p_0 = \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$.

::: {#lem-lemados}
There exists a sequence $\langle A_n : n \in \omega \rangle$ of
antichains in $\mathbb P$ such that for every $n \in \omega$:

1. $A_n$ is an infinite maximal antichain in $\mathbb P$;
2. there is $a \in A_n$ with $a \leq p_n$;
3. for every $x \in A_n$,
   $|\{y \in A_{n+1} : y \leq x\}| = \omega$; and
4. for every $y \in A_{n+1}$ there is $x \in A_n$ with $y \leq x$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Consider $p_0 \in \mathbb P$. By @lem-anticadenas, there is
$A_0 \subseteq \mathbb P$ satisfying the conditions of
@lem-anticadenas with $p = p_0 = q$.

Suppose for some $n \in \omega$ there is
$\langle A_i : i \leq n \rangle$ satisfying (1), (2), (3) and (4).
Since $A_n$ is maximal in $\mathbb P$, by @prp-equivalencia, for
some $a_n \in A_n$, $a_n \mid p_{n+1}$. Let $p = a_n$ and
$q = p_{n+1}$ in @lem-anticadenas and obtain an antichain
$A_n(a_n)$ satisfying the clauses of @lem-anticadenas.

For each $x \in A_n \setminus \{a_n\}$ let $p = x = q$ in
@lem-anticadenas to obtain an antichain $A_n(x)$ satisfying the
conditions of @lem-anticadenas.

Define $A_{n+1} = \bigcup \{A_n(x) : x \in A_n\}$ and we show that
$A_{n+1}$ satisfies (1), (2), (3) and (4).

We verify $A_{n+1}$ satisfies (1). Let $y, z \in A_{n+1}$ and
suppose $y \mid z$. Then $y \in A_n(x)$ and $z \in A_n(x')$ for some
$x, x' \in A_n$, and there is $w \in A_{n+1}$ with $w \leq y, z$.
Since $y \leq x$ and $z \leq x'$, $w \leq x, x'$, that is
$x \mid x'$, where $x, x' \in A_n$, which is an antichain, hence
$x = x'$. So $y, z \in A_n(x)$, hence $z = y$. So $A_{n+1}$ is an
antichain.

To see $A_{n+1}$ is a maximal antichain, take $r \in \mathbb P$ and
show $A_{n+1}$ satisfies the equivalence of @prp-equivalencia.
Since $A_n$ is a maximal antichain in $\mathbb P$, by
@prp-equivalencia, for some $x \in A_n$, $x \mid r$. Let
$r' \in \mathbb P$ with $r' \leq x, r$. Since $A_n(x)$ satisfies
condition (2) of @lem-anticadenas with $p = x$, there is
$a \in A_n(x)$ compatible with $r'$. So for some $a' \leq a, r'$,
$a' \leq a, r$, hence $a \mid r$.

$A_{n+1}$ satisfies (2): by construction
$A_n(a_n) \subseteq A_{n+1}$, and by @lem-anticadenas (3) there is
$a \in A_n(a_n)$ with $a \leq p_n$.

Let $x \in A_n$ and we verify (3). Our definition of $A_n(x)$
guarantees that $A_n(x) \subseteq x^{\downarrow}$ by
@lem-anticadenas (4), and by @lem-anticadenas (1),
$|A_n(x)| = \omega$. By definition of $A_{n+1}$,
$A_n(x) \subseteq A_{n+1}$, so
$|\{y \in A_{n+1} : y \leq x\}| = \omega$.

Now we prove (4). Let $y \in A_{n+1}$ be arbitrary. By definition
of $A_{n+1}$, $y \in A_n(x)$ for some $x \in A_n$, hence $y \leq x$.
:::

In the following results, the collection $\{A_n : n \in \omega\}$ is
the sequence of antichains described in @lem-lemados.

Let $\mathbb Q = \omega^{<\omega}$ and we examine the relation
between $\mathbb Q_n = \{p : \operatorname{dom} p = n+1\} \subseteq
\mathbb Q$ and $A_n \subseteq \mathbb P$ for each $n \in \omega$.

::: {#lem-biyecciones}
There exists $\langle e_i : i \in \omega \rangle$ such that for
every $i < \omega$:

1. $e_i : \mathbb Q_i \to A_i$, where $e_i$ is a bijection;
2. if $p \in \mathbb Q_{n+1}$ and $r \in \mathbb Q_i$, with
   $i \leq n$ and $p \leq r$, then $e_{n+1}(p) \leq e_i(r)$; and
3. if $p \in \mathbb Q_{n+1}$ and $r \in \mathbb Q_i$, with
   $i \leq n$, are such that $p \perp r$, then
   $e_{n+1}(p) \perp e_i(r)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By finite induction we construct the desired functions between each
$\mathbb Q_n$ and $A_n$.

We have $\mathbb Q_0 = \{p : \operatorname{dom} p = 1\}$ and
$|\mathbb Q_0| = |A_0| = \omega$. So we take $e_0$ to be any
bijection between $\mathbb Q_0$ and $A_0$.

Suppose for some $n \in \omega$ the sequence
$\langle e_i : i \leq n \rangle$ satisfies (1), (2) and (3).

For each $p \in \mathbb Q_n$ define
$\mathbb Q_n(p) = \{q \in \mathbb Q_{n+1} : q \leq p\}$.

Observe the following:

- (i) Since $\mathbb Q_n(p) = \{p^{\frown} i : i \in \omega\}$,
  $|\mathbb Q_n(p)| = \omega$.
- (ii) If $p, r \in \mathbb Q_n$ with $p \neq r$, then
  $\mathbb Q_n(p) \cap \mathbb Q_n(r) = \emptyset$. By
  contrapositive, if $q \in \mathbb Q_n(p) \cap \mathbb Q_n(r)$,
  then $q \leq p, r$, that is, $p \mid r$, hence $p = r$.
- (iii) For each $x \in A_n \subseteq \mathbb P$, define
  $A_n(x) := \{r \in A_{n+1} : r \leq x\}$. By @lem-lemados (3),
  $|A_n(x)| = \omega$, and by clause (4) of the same lemma,
  $A_{n+1} = \bigcup \{A_n(x) : x \in A_n\}$.
- (iv) $A_n(x)$ and $A_n(y)$ are disjoint whenever $x \neq y$.
  Indeed, if $r \in A_n(x) \cap A_n(y)$, then $r \in A_{n+1}$ and
  $r \leq x, y$, that is $x, y \in A_n$ are compatible, so $x = y$.

For each $p \in \mathbb Q_n$ fix a bijection
$e_n^p : \mathbb Q_n(p) \to A_n(e_n(p))$. Note by (iii),
$A_{n+1} = \bigcup \{A_n(e_n(p)) : p \in \mathbb Q_n\}$.

Let $e_{n+1} := \bigcup \{e_n^p : p \in \mathbb Q_n\}$. $e_{n+1}$ is
a function because by (ii) the domains of the $e_n^p$ are pairwise
disjoint. We now verify $e_{n+1}$ is a bijection between
$\mathbb Q_{n+1}$ and $A_{n+1}$ that also satisfies (2) and (3).

To verify (1), note first
$\operatorname{dom} e_{n+1} = \bigcup \{\operatorname{dom} e_n^p :
p \in \mathbb Q_n\}$. Since
$\operatorname{dom} e_n^p = \mathbb Q_n(p)$ for each
$p \in \mathbb Q_n$,
$\operatorname{dom} e_{n+1} = \bigcup \{\mathbb Q_n(p) :
p \in \mathbb Q_n\}$. We now prove
$\operatorname{dom} e_{n+1} = \mathbb Q_{n+1}$.

We show every element of $\operatorname{dom} e_{n+1}$ is an element
of $\mathbb Q_{n+1}$. If $p' \in \operatorname{dom} e_{n+1}$, then
$p' \in \mathbb Q_n(p)$ for some $p \in \mathbb Q_n$. But by
definition of $\mathbb Q_n(p)$, $p' \in \mathbb Q_{n+1}$, hence
$\operatorname{dom} e_{n+1} \subseteq \mathbb Q_{n+1}$.

We verify the remaining containment. If $p \in \mathbb Q_{n+1}$,
then $p \restriction n+1 \in \mathbb Q_n$ and
$p \leq p \restriction n+1$, so
$p \in \mathbb Q_n(p \restriction n+1)$, hence
$p \in \operatorname{dom} e_{n+1}$.

We show $e_{n+1}$ is injective. Let
$p_1, p_2 \in \operatorname{dom} e_{n+1}$ with $p_1 \neq p_2$. By
definition of $e_{n+1}$, there are $p, r \in \mathbb Q_n$ with
$p_1 \in \mathbb Q_n(p)$ and $p_2 \in \mathbb Q_n(r)$. If $p = r$,
then $e_n^p(p_1) \neq e_n^p(p_2)$ since $e_n^p$ is a bijection. If
$p \neq r$, then $e_n(p) \neq e_n(r)$ by the inductive hypothesis,
hence by (iv) $A_n(e_n(p)) \cap A_n(e_n(r)) = \emptyset$. Since
$e_n^p(p_1) \in A_n(e_n(p))$ and $e_n^r(p_2) \in A_n(e_n(r))$,
$e_n^p(p_1) \neq e_n^r(p_2)$. Since
$e_{n+1}(p_1) = e_n^p(p_1)$ and $e_{n+1}(p_2) = e_n^r(p_2)$, the
result follows.

Observe that
$$
\operatorname{Im}(e_{n+1}) = \bigcup \{\operatorname{Im}(e_n^p) :
p \in \mathbb Q_n\} = \bigcup \{A_n(e_n(p)) : p \in \mathbb Q_n\} =
A_{n+1}.
$$

We claim:

(v) $e_{n+1}(p) \leq e_n(p \restriction n+1)$ for every
$p \in \mathbb Q_{n+1}$. Indeed, if $p \in \mathbb Q_{n+1}$, then
$(p \restriction n+1) \in \mathbb Q_n$. Since
$p \leq p \restriction n+1 \in \mathbb Q_n$,
$p \in \mathbb Q_n(p \restriction n+1)$. So
$e_{n+1}(p) \in A_n(e_n(p \restriction n+1))$, hence
$e_{n+1}(p) \leq e_n(p \restriction n+1)$.

To prove (2), take $p \in \mathbb Q_{n+1}$ and $r \in \mathbb Q_i$
with $i \leq n$ and $p \leq r$. Since
$(p \restriction n+1) \in \mathbb Q_n$ and
$(p \restriction n+1) \leq r$, by the inductive hypothesis
$e_n(p \restriction n+1) \leq e_i(r)$. By the above and (v),
$e_{n+1}(p) \leq e_i(r)$.

It remains to prove (3). Let $p \in \mathbb Q_{n+1}$ and
$r \in \mathbb Q_i$, with $i \leq n$ and $p \perp r$.

Since $(p \restriction n+1) \in \mathbb Q_n$,
$r \perp (p \restriction n+1)$. Indeed, $p \perp r$ if and only if
$p \cup r$ is not a function, i.e. there is
$k \in \operatorname{dom} p \cap \operatorname{dom} r$ with
$p(k) \neq r(k)$. By hypothesis $i \leq n$, hence
$i + 1 \leq n + 1 = \operatorname{dom}(p \restriction n+1)$. Since
$k \in \operatorname{dom} r$, $k < i + 1 \leq n + 1$, that is,
$k \in \operatorname{dom}(p \restriction n+1) \cap
\operatorname{dom} r$. Since also
$p(k) = (p \restriction n+1)(k)$,
$(p \restriction n+1)(k) \neq r(k)$. So
$(p \restriction n+1) \perp r$ and, by the inductive hypothesis,
$e_i(r) \perp e_n(p \restriction n+1)$.

We claim $e_{n+1}(p) \perp e_i(r)$. Otherwise, there would be
$s \leq e_{n+1}(p), e_i(r)$. By (v),
$s \leq e_i(r), e_n(p \restriction n+1)$, contradicting the previous
paragraph.
:::

We are finally in a position to prove the theorem announced at the
beginning of the section.

::: {#thm-cohen}
If $\mathbb P$ is a countable atomless partial order, then
$\omega^{<\omega} \leq_d \mathbb P$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Consider the elements of the sequence
$\langle e_n : n \in \omega \rangle$ guaranteed by
@lem-biyecciones.

Let $e := \big(\bigcup_{n \in \omega} e_n\big) \cup
            \{(\emptyset, \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P})\}$.

We have $\operatorname{dom} e =
\bigcup_{n \in \omega} \operatorname{dom} e_n \cup \{\emptyset\} =
\bigcup_{n \in \omega} \mathbb Q_n \cup \{\emptyset\} =
\omega^{<\omega}$. Now,
$\operatorname{Im}(e) = \bigcup_{n \in \omega} \operatorname{Im}(e_n)
\cup \{\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}\} = \bigcup_{n \in \omega} A_n \cup
\{\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}\}$.

We claim $e : \omega^{<\omega} \to \mathbb P$ is a dense embedding.

Indeed, $e$ is a function because for every $n, m \in \omega$,
$n \neq m$ implies
$\mathbb Q_n \cap \mathbb Q_m = \emptyset$. Indeed, if
$p \in \mathbb Q_n \cap \mathbb Q_m$, then by definition of
$\mathbb Q_n$ and $\mathbb Q_m$, $\operatorname{dom} p = n+1$ and
$\operatorname{dom} p = m+1$, hence $n = m$.

Let $p \in \mathbb P$ and we show $\operatorname{Im}(e)$ is dense in
$\mathbb P$. Recall that, before @lem-lemados, we fixed an
enumeration of $\mathbb P$. So $p = p_k$ for some $k \in \omega$. By
@lem-lemados (2), there is $a \in A_k$ with $a \leq p_k$. So
$a \in \operatorname{Im}(e)$ and $a \leq p_k$.

Let $p, q \in \omega^{<\omega}$ with $p \leq q$ and we prove $e$
preserves the order. We start with the trivial cases. If
$q = \emptyset$, then $e(p) \leq e(q)$ since
$e(q) := \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$. If $q \neq \emptyset$ and $p = q$,
then $e(p) = e(q)$, so the result holds. Suppose then that
$p < q$ with $q \neq \emptyset$. Let $\operatorname{dom} p = m + 1$
and $\operatorname{dom} q = i + 1$. Since $p < q$,
$i + 1 < m + 1$, hence $i < m$. Letting $n := m - 1$ gives
$i \leq n$ and $n + 1 = m$. So by @lem-biyecciones (2),
$e_m(p) \leq e_i(q)$. But by definition of $e$, $e(p) = e_m(p)$ and
$e(q) = e_i(q)$. So $e(p) \leq e(q)$.

We prove $e$ preserves incompatibility. Let
$p, q \in \omega^{<\omega}$ with $p \perp q$. Observe that neither
$p$ nor $q$ is the empty function, since for every
$s \in \omega^{<\omega}$, $s \leq \emptyset$, in particular
$s \mid \emptyset$. So there are $m, i \in \omega$ with
$p \in \mathbb Q_m$ and $q \in \mathbb Q_i$. If $m = i$, then
$p, q \in \mathbb Q_m$, so by @lem-biyecciones (1)
$e_m(p) \neq e_m(q)$ and $e_m(p), e_m(q) \in A_m$. Hence
$e_m(p) \perp e_m(q)$, that is, $e(p) \perp e(q)$.

Now, if $m \neq i$, WLOG assume $m > i$. So letting $n := m - 1 \geq
i$, $n + 1 = m$, hence $p \in \mathbb Q_{n+1}$ and $q \in
\mathbb Q_i$ with $i \leq n$. By @lem-biyecciones (3),
$e_m(p) \perp e_i(q)$, that is, $e(p) \perp e(q)$.
:::

Orders of type $\operatorname{Fn}(\omega, 2)$ and
$\operatorname{Fn}(\omega, \omega)$ are countable and atomless. The
latter is verified: if, for example,
$p \in \operatorname{Fn}(\omega, 2)$, since $|p| < \omega$ and
$\operatorname{dom} p \subseteq \omega$, we can take
$n \in \omega \setminus \operatorname{dom} p$. Then
$r = p \cup \{(n, 0)\}$ and $q = p \cup \{(n, 1)\}$ are two
incompatible extensions of $p$ in $\operatorname{Fn}(\omega, 2)$.
The same argument shows that $\operatorname{Fn}(\omega, \omega)$ is
atomless. Likewise, $2^{<\omega}$ is a countable atomless partial
order (see the comments after @def-concatenacion). So as a corollary
of the previous theorem, all such orders produce the same generic
extension as $\omega^{<\omega}$.

It is interesting to observe that in @thm-cohen the countability
hypothesis on $\mathbb P$ cannot be dropped.

To verify this, consider an infinite cardinal $\kappa$ and the orders
$2^{<\omega}$ and $\operatorname{Fn}(\kappa, 2)$. We view
$2^{<\omega}$ as a suborder of $\operatorname{Fn}(\kappa, 2)$.

Observe that in this case the inclusion
$i : 2^{<\omega} \to \operatorname{Fn}(\kappa, 2)$ is a complete
embedding. $i$ preserves order and incompatibility trivially. Using
the equivalence of @thm-equivalenciaencaje, we verify that every
element of $\operatorname{Fn}(\kappa, 2)$ admits an $i$-reduction to
$2^{<\omega}$. Let $q \in \operatorname{Fn}(\kappa, 2)$. Then
$|\omega \cap \operatorname{dom} q| < \omega$, so there is
$n \in \omega$ with
$(\omega \cap \operatorname{dom} q) \subseteq n$. We claim the
function $r : n \to 2$ defined by
$$
r(m) = \begin{cases} q(m), & \text{if } m \in \operatorname{dom} q, \\
                     0,    & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$
is an $i$-reduction of $q$ to $2^{<\omega}$. Let $p \leq r$, i.e.
$r \subseteq p$. We prove $i(p) = p$ is compatible with $q$, that
is, $p \cup q$ is a function. Take
$m \in \operatorname{dom} p \cap \operatorname{dom} q$. Then
$m \in \operatorname{dom} p \in \omega$ and
$m \in \operatorname{dom} q$, hence $r(m) = q(m)$. Since
$r \subseteq p$, $p(m) = r(m)$, hence $p(m) = q(m)$, which proves
the claim.

So $2^{<\omega} \leq_c \operatorname{Fn}(\kappa, 2)$. By
@thm-encajeuno, the generic extension given by
$\operatorname{Fn}(\kappa, 2)$ contains the one given by
$2^{<\omega}$. Since @prp-unnuevoreal says forcing with
$2^{<\omega}$ adds a new real, the forcing notion
$\operatorname{Fn}(\kappa, 2)$ does too.

Let $\mathbb P := \{p : p \subseteq \kappa \times 2 \,\&\,
p \text{ is a function} \,\&\, |p| \leq \omega\}$, and
$\mathbb Q := \operatorname{Fn}(\kappa, 2)$, both ordered by
reverse inclusion.

For the rest of our example we assume $\kappa^{\omega} = \kappa$.
This property is held, for example, by the continuum $\mathfrak{c}$.
In other words: if $\kappa = \mathfrak{c} = 2^{\omega}$, then
$\kappa^{\omega} = (2^{\omega})^{\omega} = 2^{\omega} = \mathfrak{c}$.

The proof of @prp-nadanuevo is easily adapted to prove that
$\mathbb P$ does not add new functions from $\omega$ to $2$.

Observe that $|\mathbb P| = \kappa = |\mathbb Q|$. Note
$\{\{(\alpha, 0)\} : \alpha < \kappa\}$ is a subset of both
$\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$. So both have cardinality at least
$\kappa$. Now, $\mathbb P \subseteq [\kappa \times 2]^{\leq \omega}$,
so $|\mathbb P| \leq |[\kappa \times 2]^{\leq \omega}| =
|[\kappa]^{\leq \omega}| = \kappa^{\omega} = \kappa$.

Likewise, since $\mathbb Q \subseteq [\kappa \times 2]^{<\omega}$,
$|\mathbb Q| \leq |[\kappa \times 2]^{<\omega}| \leq \kappa$.

Finally, both $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ are atomless: if
$p \in \mathbb P$, take
$\alpha \in \kappa \setminus \operatorname{dom} p$. Then
$r = p \cup \{(\alpha, 0)\}$ and $q = p \cup \{(\alpha, 1)\}$ are
two incompatible extensions of $p$ in $\mathbb P$. The same
argument shows $\mathbb Q$ is atomless.

So $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ are two uncountable atomless partial
orders, neither densely embedded in the other: otherwise,
$\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ would produce the same generic
extensions, which is impossible since $\mathbb P$ does not add new
functions from $\omega$ to $2$ while $\mathbb Q$ does.
